This study introduces a novel time series model called TV-PARX, which is based on a time-varying Poisson process and is designed to handle potentially nonlinear dynamics and sudden changes in the data. To estimate the model parameters, we utilize a generic method called EM and to forecast, we use a quasi-maximum likelihood approach. To validate the effectiveness of the TV-PARX model, we apply it to simulate and forecast the global air traffic patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic, demonstrating its capability to predict structural breaks in the data.

On September 16, 2020, a calibration-free method for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth was tested using wide-field photometry data collected by the Pierre Auger Observatory's fluorescence and charged particle detectors. What drove the approach was the understanding that extended particle showers produced by high-energy cosmic rays in the atmosphere would not significantly alter the photometry determinations made by both detectors, as confirmed by simulations and a consistency with theoretical predictions regarding the hadronic interaction model used. A constant relationship between the aerosol optical depth and the blue wavelength, observed empirically and explained by a lack of significant aerosol emission in the visible spectrum, allowed for a linear fit to be applied to the data, yielding a value of 0.10 ± 0.02 for the vertical aerosol optical depth without requiring absolute calibration of the detectors. This result aligns with previous measurements and is consistent with local meteorological data and global climatology patterns. A breakdown of the source of uncertainties was provided, with the main uncertainty stemming from the determination of the linear fit's slope, followed by calibration and measurement uncertainties. The approach's advantages and limitations were discussed, and a proposal was made for future wide-field detectors to employ this method for monitoring local weather conditions, starting with the upgraded "AugerPrime" experiment which will feature improved surface detectors with enhanced sensitivity in the bluer part of the spectrum.

This study compares three molecular dynamics simulation methods—Langevin dynamics and Hamiltonian dynamics, as well as their implicit solvent representations—on a biomolecular system, specifically alanine dipeptide. Furthermore, it explores the system's conformational landscape using both explicit and implicit solvents.

This research project resulted in creating new guidelines for automatically generating descriptions of images, building on the existing ImageNet descriptions. The purpose of these descriptions is to aid visually impaired users and thus the new guidelines were crafted with descriptive standards that benefit this specific group. The initiative began with translating key concepts from the ICDAP 2017 guidelines into a more effective and usable format for deep learning. The revised descriptions were created using a combination of automated methods and human input, and their performance was assessed through experiments. The new description standards were then published on existing image databases and described various categories not yet described. Ultimately, the project contributed to the ICDAR 2019 conference by delivering a concept cluster with enhanced descriptive standards and a searchable dataset accessible online.

This research focuses on an unconventional optimization technique in quantum field theory, specifically related to operator construction and parameter estimation. We utilize Euler-Arnold equations, leveraging their non-local characteristic through an anisotropic metric analitysis, and implement this method for a scalar field under anisotropic conditions. Through an example of spin-1 particle detection and by examining the anisotropic Heisenberg uncertainty principle, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

The evolution of hard-scattered heavy quarks within a stellar context is examined, drawing on a mean-field approach based on a specific model of Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP). By solving the Boltzmann equation, we determine the distribution of heavy quarks transverse to the flow direction for various masses. In an interaction model where the constituent heavy quark contributes to its own inertia, we find that significant in-equilibrium heating results in chiral mass reduction. By linking constituent and current quark masses, we obtain the heavy quark distribution across different masses. Our models of charm and bottom quark in-equilibrium distributions align well with existing theoretical and experimental data, supporting the validity of the quasi-universal chiral mass redistribution function.

This work addresses the problem of optimizing throughput in wideband waveforming, focusing on throughput fairness and overall throughput, under general conditions where throughput varies non-linearly with bandwidth allocated. We model this allocation issue as a resource distribution task and develop a fair-throughput optimization algorithm with polynomial time complexity, applicable to both linear and non-linear throughput functions. Additionally, we propose an integer programming formulation for fair-throughput optimization and prove its optimal throughputs are equivalent in general and non-linear scenarios. We also introduce an efficient fair-throughput optimization method that requires fewer computations compared to existing approaches, particularly in cases with multiple users. Finally, we validate our findings using a simulated environment with non-linear throughput characteristics.

PDF fitting involves obtaining a function that accurately represents data collected at various scales, with dglap evolution playing a key role in connecting and comparing data points. This paper presents an approach using neural network operators to model pdfs and incorporates dglap evolution to ensure consistency across scales. Our method is shown to be capable of accurately predicting data points at untrained scales while allowing for exploration of different scale-dependent outcomes. Furthermore, the approach is verified to be consistent with the dglap evolution equations and can be utilized for probabilistic regression of scale-dependent data, making it a valuable tool for data analysis.

A novel k-epsilon combustion model is integrated into a basic Gaussian mean flow model, enabling an analysis of how fuel burns in turbulent, premixed flames using linear stability theory. A third-order difference scheme is employed to accurately compute derivatives within the stability analysis. The modified model is then compared to the standard model, showing that the new model performs better within the linear framework. To validate the findings, the model is used to predict the growth of disturbances in premixed flames at various Reynolds numbers, comparing the results to direct numerical simulation data, and finding good agreement.

This study focuses on a nonlocal gravity theory where acceleration at any given point is influenced by the distribution of mass both locally and globally. To make this theory consistent with general relativity, a nonlocal constitutive relation is proposed. Its validity is verified by showing that the globally influenced acceleration aligns with the Ramathudu-Eddington equation, ensuring the theory's applicability to observed phenomena. Since the equation holds globally, it is also applicable in scenarios with significant mass concentrations, such as galaxies, in contrast to theories of nonlocal gravity that show success only in weak field conditions. We derive the expression for the constitutive relation in the context of scalar field theory and demonstrate its equivalence to speed-of-light theory proposed by Shaw and Mottaghi.

A notable trend observed recently is the heightened production of strange quarks
seen in high-multiplicity elementary collisions, which mirrors the behavior
of particles formed in the center of a theoretical particle type, the quark-gluon plasma.
A theoretical framework, hydrodynamics, fails to explain this phenomenon without
incorporating an uncharacteristic level of energy loss for strange quarks.
However, an alternative explanation involving the direct conversion of energy within
collisions, which typically results in heavy particles, could reasonably account for
the enhanced production of strange quarks and their related properties.
A computer-generated table of proton-proton collisions at various energy levels
is examined to verify the conservation of energy and to verify the consistent behavior
of the system before and upon strangeness enhancement.

To accurately predict the number of neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (NS-LMXBs) present in the Galaxy, we need to examine various mechanisms that can transform them into millisecond radio pulsars (MSPs). We focused on three primary transformation processes: binary rejuvenation through mass transfer, disruption due to gravitational waves, and disruptions following stellar or giant planet close encounters. We also considered the possibility of transformation failures caused by white dwarf companions entering an unstable accretion state or significant mass loss resulting in companion ejection. By taking these factors into account, we aimed to match the nearly confirmed population of neutron star LMXRBs observed in the Milky Way, including both visible and invisible populations, along with their tidal disk disruptions, as reported by Chandra and XMM-Newton. To achieve this, we developed a population synthesis model that aligns with the MSP and their recycled pulsar populations, as well as their binary counterparts discovered by Parkes, and the observed population of Hulse-Taylor pulsars, consistent with both Field and Rasio (1998) and Tauris and Brown (2002) predictions. The desired population of transformed NS-LMXBs requires binary rejuvenation to play a crucial role, while the observed MSP population demands significant disruption rates due to gravitational wave interactions and close encounters, along with a binary system formation rate of around 2 per year, consistent with recent predictions from the Milky Way's stellar remnant populations. A bipartite graph can be represented in a planar manner by breaking select points into smaller components, where the number of such components is bounded logarithmically based on the graph's maximum degree. This result is derived from a more initial finding that applies to all graphs, indicating that a nearly 2-powerful function of the graph's size through which, by similarly breaking points into smaller components, a planar representation can be achieved.

Degrading cache performance is necessary for successful Flush-Reload attacks to reveal memory contents. Traditional methods like Flush-ReloadS and Brown-Out rely on reducing cache efficiency globally within a CPU core, which is slow to execute and prone to heat buildup. On the other hand, targeting specific caches like L1 or L2 for degradation has been shown to be even slower and not always effective. We introduce HyperDegrade, a technique that focuses on specific sets of cache lines within specific caches, making it more efficient. We also present a new way to reorganize the execution of degradation and measurement cycles, balancing the need for effective degradation with the need to collect high-quality readings. Experiments on Intel and AMD CPUs show that HyperDegrade is at least 33% more efficient in terms of line contents recovery and can be up to two orders of magnitude faster in some cases compared to Brown-Out. We also introduce a new execution pattern called the Ping-Pong pattern, which alternates between degradation and measurement cycles on different cache sets, showing further improvements that can be significant, especially with longer execution times. The Ping-Pong pattern leads to better efficiency by allowing for more accurate cache readability after degradation, reducing the need for extensive warm-up periods. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of HyperDegrade as a powerful tool for memory attacks with fine-grained time details, making it more susceptible to attacks like those based on Flush-Reload techniques.

A new variant of the conventional 21-move theorem for knot theory is introduced here, termed the 11-move theorem. This updated theorem posits that any intricately knotted graph can be simplified to its most basic form through a sequence of cutting, splitting, gluing, and 11-move transformations. Notably, this process can be achieved without diagonal moves and by utilizing an enhanced version of the standard sequence-point reduction, which involves an 11-move transformation equivalent to both the standard 11-move and the recently developed diagonal move. Building on the 11-move theorem, we also develop an algorithm to determine the minimum number of times two closed curves intersect when gluing pairs of intervals on various basic loop structures.

This study investigates how learning rate and task difficulty distribution influence the performance of two collaborative strategies employed by binary classifiers in a multi-agent setup. The setup involves multiple agents, each making irreversible decisions based on noisy feedback about an unknown characteristic. The research aims to balance the need for information to optimize future decisions and the desire to take action for immediate benefits. Through computational experiments, the study provides insights on when specific strategies work best and establishes performance guarantees for them. The results obtained contribute to the understanding of optimal decision-making processes in collaborative settings by theoretical information.

A simultaneous action of groups is considered regular when no non-trivial subgroup pairs differ except in one position. We establish that regular simultaneous actions of groups on a space can be fully organized into structured components, and we derive a method for calculating the total count of component sets. As an application, when the involved groups are identical and the space is one-dimensional, we show that the overall structure aligns with a power of the group only if all subgroups of varying sizes are cyclic and commute within themselves. Otherwise, we propose a novel structure that incorporates how subgroups of different sizes arrange and position themselves.

A novel design for a sagnac interferometer has been developed to address the sensitivity limitations encountered in traditional sagnac interferometers, particularly those used in gravitational wave detectors. This redesigned sloshing-Sagnic interferometer achieves a 100-fold enhancement in sensitivity by alternating the flow direction of the laser beam within the sagnac loop, complemented by an integrated sloshing-Sagnac controller that optimizes the configuration for maximum sensitivity. A theoretical analysis of this design's performance reveals that, given identical parameters, the sloshing-Sagnic interferometer offers a sensitivity improvement of approximately 10 times compared to a conventional sagnac interferometer, making this innovative design highly pertinent to the evolving needs of gravitational wave detectors and other systems employing sagnac interferometers.

To enhance random access efficiency in systems with extremely large MIMO arrays, we've developed an improved version of the NOVR protocol, termed NOVR-XL, specifically designed for XL-MIMO systems with a fractional time slot structure. In the proposed framework, multiple users transmitting the same data packet concurrently to the base station result in a combined signal, enabling successful recovery and retransmission without individual user feedback, similar to what's described in [10]. However, unlike the approach in [10], our proposed protocol allows for a fractional time slot structure, providing improved efficiency, and incorporates a multi-slot based NOVR-based protocol, termed NOVR-XL, for initial transmission and potential retransmissions. Through theoretical analysis and computer simulations, we've demonstrated the advantages of the proposed protocol in terms of successful access probability and average access delay compared to existing protocols. Furthermore, in the limit of an infinitely large array size, we've shown that the proposed protocol can emulate an ideal instantaneous access system with no collision problems.

This research tackles the issue of low accuracy in neural language models when handling rare words during machine translation and summarization tasks. We propose a new model that integrates $n$-gram statistics with neural language modeling to machine translation output, utilizing an optimization-based method to determine the best output sequence. Our approach allows for smooth integration of $n$-gram and neural models with any probability encoding method, including arithmetic coding. Our tests, conducted on English and Chinese news machine translation tasks as well as English news summarization, demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms previous techniques by significantly reducing the optimal translation sequence optimization error. Our method also shows promising results when using high-precision probability encoding with machine translation output.

Effective data entry and management are crucial for an electronic vote tabulation system that utilizes handwriting recognition. To enhance the performance of this system, which employs an OCR-based Mexican handwriting alphabet, a sophisticated error-correction technique was implemented. This technique, based on grammatical analysis and utilizing an n-gram language model with a bigram level, helps minimize recognition mistakes. Furthermore, evaluating language probabilities is crucial in identifying and correcting potential errors. The system's efficiency was enhanced by integrating a real-time spell-checker that operates on the fly. A comprehensive evaluation of the spell-correction technique's effectiveness was conducted, and the system's overall performance was assessed through extensive testing.

This study investigates the circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere modified to mimic current Martian atmospheric conditions, focusing on large-scale events similar to baroclinic storms observed on Mars. General circulation models were employed to conduct a set of experiments with the modified atmosphere, featuring both constant and varying solar radiation levels, to explore the structure of the new circulation system that emerges. Results from experiments with constant solar radiation levels show that high-latitude direct circulation develops initially, followed by a transition to a three-cell circulation pattern as the system stabilizes, mirroring the circulation patterns observed on Mars. Time-dependent experiments with varying solar radiation levels reveal that baroclinic storms similar to those on Mars can be triggered and that their intensity grows with more extreme seasonal changes, showing behavior consistent with seasonal cycles on Mars. The three-cell circulation system is found to be robust against seasonal changes, demonstrating stability across varying sol cycles, and it is concluded that three-cell circulation is the predominant large-scale circulation pattern in the modified atmosphere. This study provides a framework for understanding the circulation patterns in the Martian atmosphere and lays the groundwork for further investigations into the behavior of atmospheres with three-cell circulation systems, including the exploration of seasonal cycles and dust storms on Mars as well as seasonal cycles observed on Titan.

Special functions such as the Gamma function can be effectively represented within the framework of complex analysis. Using Phragmen-Lindelof estimates, we outline a straightforward Hankel path for constructing a variant of the Gamma function, and we demonstrate its equivalence to the standard Riemann-Schneider definition and an analogous variant of the Beta function. Our proof of the Gamma function's logarithmic convexity on the positive real line relies on an even simpler integration path for the function's definition, and we provide a straightforward extension of the function to include zero and negative integers with an exact normalization constant. We also derive the Gamma function's fundamental recurrence relation and establish its connection to Euler's product and infinite power series representations, as well as an asymptotic one. Furthermore, we define an analogous function for quaternionic and more broadly, Banach space variables, and we outline an alternative, direct derivation of the Beta function from the gamma function, along with an integration formula that extends the Beta function to arbitrary positive real numbers.

This research presents a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method for quantum many-body systems that easily integrates with existing hydrodynamic schemes to handle non-equilibrium situations. The linearized approach focuses on correlating quantum fluctuations using a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic equation, which accounts for pressure and viscous forces driven by non-equilibrium conditions. Testing the linearized stochastic relativistic hydrodynamic scheme using a EFT-based equation of state reveals minimal bias in simulating spinodal instabilities within neutron-rich matter. Notably, the method effectively captures complex, highly turbulent flows and validates its efficiency in reproducing non-equilibrium quantum many-body correlations, especially at low $k$, by comparing results with DNS-QMC and VMC equilibrium data. Moreover, the linearized stochastic hydrodynamic approach accurately replicates the elevated correlations, particularly the oscillations, that arise due to the spinodal instability within the flowing matter, particularly at $k \approx 1\,\mathrm{fm}^{-1}$, matching the outcomes of a fully quantum many-body DNS simulation. This successful outcome validates the linearized stochastic hydrodynamic method's capability to effectively simulate non-equilibrium situations while preserving the quantum many-body effects and hydrodynamic collective behaviors, offering a computationally efficient framework for future research on complex, turbulent flows in heavy ion collisions.

Teacher-Student (T-S) knowledge distillation has proven effective in reducing the size of a neural network while maintaining its performance, with a large deep "teacher" network guiding a smaller "student" network. Traditional T-S approaches work well when the student network is smaller but not as when it is significantly reduced compared to the teacher network. To address this challenge, our proposed High-Resolution Knowledge Distillation (HKD) framework integrates a multi-branched side network within the student architecture to capture and retain more information, allowing it to better emulate the teacher network. Additionally, we introduce advanced reduction techniques for both the teacher network and side network to further optimize performance. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that HKD enables multiple student networks to match or even surpass the teacher network in accuracy with significant reductions in computation cost, showcasing remarkable distillation gains.

To effectively manage complex graphical models with numerous variables, we adapt the Bucket Elimination algorithm to serve as a backbone for both optimizing and precisely determining the best possible outcomes. By integrating the enhanced algorithm with caching techniques and cutting branches in the search tree, we create an efficient system capable of handling large-scale models. Our modified Bucket Enhanced Backwards Elimination system successfully manages models with thousands of variables, demonstrating its ability to handle real-world scenarios such as video surveillance systems and large-scale modeling projects with success rates exceeding 99.5%.

We provide a method to compute the dimension of centralizer varieties $Z(n)(SL_2)$ for groups $SL_d$ with $d > 2$. First, we derive a formula for the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of centralizer varieties $Z(n)(SL_2)$, then we extend it to groups $SL_d$. The formula for $SL_2$ group is obtained by factoring the Cayley-Ore numerator, involving a detailed analysis of its roots. We adapt the approach for $SL_d$ groups, requiring a more complicated root analysis. As an application, we determine the asymptotic behavior of centralizer variety dimensions for $SL_d$ groups.

This study compares two methods for calculating p-values in paired-permutation tests: an previously existing exact algorithm and a newly developed exact algorithm. The purpose is to evaluate the efficiency of the new approach. The comparison focuses on the computational time required for processing various data sets with different sizes under different numbers of permutations. The results show that the new exact algorithm results in lower computational times compared to the commonly used Monte Carlo approximation, particularly with larger sample sizes. The research has practical implications for statistics, data science, machine learning, computer science, and cryptography by highlighting a more efficient method for calculating p-values in paired-permutation tests.

A consistent pattern has been observed in transverse momentum ($p_T$) distributions of hadrons, for both elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular ($v_3$) flow coefficients, indicating a similar dependence. This consistent trend was examined using hydro+initial-state scatters (ISCs) and the reaction plane (RP) method to determine flows. When implementing a $p_T$-dependent viscosity to entropy density ratio ($\eta/s$)) in hydro models, the $v_3$ distribution patterns matching those of $v_2$ required significantly more aggressive steps. Additionally, a brief overview of constitutive and non-constitutive approaches for handling $p_T$-dependent transport properties is presented.

This research addresses a scenario where a mobile vehicle navigates an area to find and confirm the presence of targets, specifically focusing on targets that remain beyond the vehicle's detection range. We propose a control policy designed to minimize the number of undetected targets within the area, utilizing deep reinforcement learning. Moreover, we develop an approximate dynamic programming method to evaluate the performance of the control policy. A case study is presented to demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed control policy and approximation method.

Computer games played over networks have become very popular and competitive, and this paper focuses on creating strategies for these games, particularly the soccer video game FIFA 14. By treating the game as a decision-making problem similar to those faced by artificial intelligence systems, the researchers used deep learning and policy gradient techniques to develop self-play training and a novel team control assessment based on game statistics. The resulting neural network-based controller outperformed previous strategies and human-controlled teams, demonstrating the effectiveness of the approach.

This study focuses on utilizing control theory to automate complex scientific experiments, particularly in astrophysics, due to the impacts of global pandemics that led to reduced laboratory access and heightened telework requirements. The goal is to develop an adaptive experimental framework that can manage sophisticated remote setups. The proposed system leverages the closure of state-space caused by experimental settings, enabling automated error checking and the organization of experiment outcomes without requiring extensive analysis. Applying this method to telescope experiments reveals its effectiveness in navigating complex setups and allows for efficient exploration of parameter spaces, even in scenarios with limited data points, as demonstrated through simulations of various experimental configurations used to investigate the neutrino sky.

This study investigates a system of solitary wave solutions that remain stable under specific conditions, influenced by an anharmonic oscillator within a one-dimensional framework. The system's governing equations are given as $\begin{cases} -\varphi'' + \varphi - \varphi^3 = \mu \varphi^2 & \\ \varphi(\pm \infty) = 1,\end{cases}$ where oscillations occur around the state $\varphi(\infty) = 1$. Building on previous research, we demonstrate that small anharmonic oscillators contribute to the stability of these solitary waves from a perspective of orbital stability. Additionally, we derive the asymptotic behavior of the solitary wave near infinity as $\varphi(x) \sim 1 - C_-\exp(\sqrt{\mu}\,|x|)$ as $|x|\rightarrow \infty$.

The effectiveness of searches for exotic particles at colliders depends significantly on their possible decay patterns, particularly for neutral long-lived particles (NLSPs) produced in sparticle decays. The "two-step" model, used to design new searches at hadron colliders, consists of initial selections to retain potential signal events and subsequent offline analyses to identify displaced vertices within the detector. To improve the efficiency of new searches, a refined trigger system is necessary that can accurately detect unusual decay patterns, specifically those occurring beyond a certain distance from the production point. A key factor in determining the optimal settings for this adapted trigger system is the decay distance of the particle, necessitating a set of optimized triggers with varying thresholds to cover all possible particle decay scenarios, similar to what is currently employed at hadron colliders.

This study provides a new quantitative measure for assessing semantic shifts in context-based word embeddings and finds that most observed shifts align with standard lexical statistics. The research also reveals that contextual variance adjustments can greatly enhance the effectiveness of existing explanations for word embedding semantics. Furthermore, the study develops a contextual embedding model that maintains the benefits of standard lexical statistics while preserving the benefits of the proposed adjustment. The results obtained support the lexical statistic-driven interpretation of semantic scales and highlight the importance of accurate data curation and initial settings in context-based learning approaches.

Based on current observations, a notable fraction of dark matter consists of potentially lightest types of particles that are extremely ultra-light. Analyzing the resultless portions of parameter space that remain for these particles that are extremely ultra-light, we are finding that modest additions of darkness that are slightly heavier, possibly lightest particles that are somewhat ultra-light, are not consistent with the distinct values of the particle that is somewhat ultra-light that are not yet explained. It's also worth noting that we are translating the results on the unexplained values of the particle that is somewhat ultra-light to those of the particle that is slightly heavier that is not yet observed, and we are obtaining tighter bounds on the mass of the particle that is slightly heavier that is not yet observed, based on the results already established for the particle that is extremely ultra-light that is not yet explained.

This study investigates how driven quantum systems, specifically Rabi and Jaynes-Cummings models, maintain their dynamic behavior under small perturbations, using the concept of dynamic coherent states to predict this stability. Time-dependent numerical simulations are employed to validate these findings. Building upon previous research, we extend our analysis to more complex scenarios by incorporating time-varying control and driving forces, as well as generalized driving protocols, while also considering the generalized Jaynes-Cummings model. A unified framework is established, linking driving protocols to specific outcomes, and a novel exponential driving protocol is introduced and analyzed. Furthermore, the impact of initial state conditions on outcome efficiency is examined, and optimal outcomes are determined for both the Rabi and Jaynes-Cummings models. Notably, in the context of the Jaynes-Cummings model, general coherence is shown to be optimal under specific conditions. Overall, our findings leverage the framework of dynamic coherent states to offer valuable insights into the stability and efficiency of driven quantum systems.

Quantum relational Hoare logic employs real numbers to describe inputs and outputs, using them to define relationships between a program's inputs and outputs. This approach is demonstrated through implementation of this logic via an API written in Python, with specifications defined in the quantum relational Hoare logic itself.

To enhance the accuracy of vector magnetic field maps, especially in regions with strong fields, we need to take into consideration magnetic fills that are less than one. This requirement led to developing a regularizing function that takes into account measurements of Ca II H and HeI 5876 Å chromospheric lines, which are sensitive to both thermal and magnetic conditions, in addition to creating fill fraction spectra across the entire vector magnetic field map. This paper presents a novel method for incorporating fills that are less than one in energy function calculations and describes the algorithm used to determine vector magnetic fields, which includes considering those factors as well as Ca II H and HeI line profiles, in addition to UV and visible continuum fluctuations, to determine thermal fields before deriving vector fields. Vector magnetic field measurements of active regions shown in this work align well with observed features, and the method's effectiveness was also confirmed through a comparison with other approaches, demonstrating that considering those factors results in low-fill fraction regions with strong fields, consistent with cause-effect relationships between flux tubes that are highly concentrated and chromospheric mass and energy collapses that give rise to phenomena such as spicules, bright points, and flares.

A Coxeter group can be visualized as a collection of spheres arranged in a half-plane, where each sphere reflects across a line to potentially generate new spheres, or more new ones if not on the boundary. If multiple spheres are placed in a section of the half-plane between two lines forming an angle, reflection can spread them out. We define the set containing all spheres resulting from this process within the same section. Let's denote the maximum radius a sphere can have as R and the number of initial spheres as n. The defining parameters for this subset of the Coxeter group are then (n+1) and 2^R. We provide proof that this subset forms a group and calculate the total number of distinct points on its boundary. Furthermore, if the angle between the two lines is not a specific rational multiple of pi, we consider the case where infinitely many spheres are created, and we determine the set of all possible radii for these spheres.

Bertrand curves are defined on manifolds of codimension 1 in codimensions greater than 1. When studying these curves, we examine their properties within the Frenet-Sarnd spaces. In these specific areas, we demonstrate that the concept of Bertrand curves applies only to codimension 1.

Multi-task learning aims to enable AI models to simultaneously learn several related tasks. Despite its many benefits, the field has largely focused on well-behaved objectives such as mean squared error and regression tasks. However, in real-world applications, researchers have found that using objectives like KL Divergence, which are difficult to optimize, can actually lead to worse performance compared to more traditional methods. To address this challenge, we propose a new technique called MPO that uses Poisson Disk Sampling to better optimize multi-task learning objectives. Our approach also introduces a scaled gradient adjustment to further improve optimization and comes with theoretical guarantees on convergence. Experiments on six different visual tasks demonstrated that our proposed method, when using KL Divergence to optimize multiple tasks, outperforms existing techniques and can even obviated the need for traditional hyperparameter tuning.

Symbolic rules characterizing specific AI behaviors are easily understandable and verifiable, making behaviors such as if-then relationships highly amenable to precise definition through neural network training. A standout study showed that a neural model could accurately identify these if-then rules without explicit training, demonstrating innate capacity to recognize hierarchical structures within the data. Building on this discovery, we developed a training framework called HET, allowing neural networks to learn the precise if-then rules by leveraging the hierarchical structure of different relationship categories. Applying this model to a vast set of undocumented behavioral patterns in two large language models of GPT, (GPT-J and GPT-3), we found the models inherently capable of exhibiting behaviors like image color transformation and object displacement through training, with the structure of relationship types further enhancing accuracy. Notably, a crucial finding revealed that neural networks can exhibit complex behaviors requiring multiple sequential actions, such as shape transformation followed by displacement, by exploiting the hierarchical organization of the training data. The identified behaviors align with a universal structure, demonstrating the capability to learn hierarchical organization of behavior categories through the training data itself.

To enable a neural network to predict videos from novel viewpoints at test time, we utilize a novel dual representation consisting of weights and biases applied to the features learned by the network. This approach uses gradient descent to determine the optimal combination of features that maximizes the output for a given novel viewpoint. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on videos of vehicles and animals, without requiring any videos from novel viewpoints during training. Furthermore, our approach has a clear geometric interpretation, revealing that videos of objects with regular patterns are more easily generalizable.

This research explores the impact of modifying a graph's structure by limiting the maximum distance between nodes, or diameter, on a specific property called the metric dimension. Initially introduced by Devienne and Germain in 2021, the concept involves analyzing graphs derived from original connected graphs by applying this modification. We present upper bound formulas for the metric dimension of these adjusted graphs and conduct comparisons with existing bounds. Through examples, we demonstrate the significance of these new bounds and provide a strengthened version of the modified diameter formula. Additionally, we offer an algorithm to compute the modified dimension efficiently in polynomial time.

This study presents a novel approach for identifying various cardiac issues in noisy environments without using any pre-trained models. Our proposed method, which operates in an end-to-end manner, utilizes a combination of the Fast Fourier Transform and a simple neural network consisting of two layers to accomplish the task of spectrogram-based classification. The system was trained and tested on the PhysioNet/CinC 2017 sound classification dataset, and our results show that it outperforms the winning entry of that contest, achieving a performance level of 75.4% in the problem domain. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robustness in detecting various cardiac abnormalities within the signal.

To investigate the role of low-density environments around extreme starburst galaxies, we analyzed the ratios of recurrent Tatelle emission lines ($7.49\mu$m / $8.06$um) for 21 local galaxies and compared the results with theoretical models. Notably, we examined how these ratios might be influenced by circumgalactic gas reservoirs or low-density molecular outflows. Additionally, we developed a simple ratio-based model to estimate outflow velocities for the most intense starburst galaxies. Our analysis suggests that the most extreme cases, such as 30 Dor and NGC 253, might be better explained by circumgalactic reservoirs rather than outflows. However, we concluded that more detailed spectral observations and a deeper understanding of line emissions are necessary to make reliable diagnoses of low-density molecular environments.

Data collected from real-world conditions often contains inconsistencies and gaps that don't align with the underlying models, especially during significant events like the recent global pandemic. Handling and filling these issues effectively is crucial for building accurate epidemiological models. This research introduces a biological feasibility constraint based on basic epidemiological principles to address missing and erroneous data. We present a discrete-time differential equation model and develop a data processing technique, supported by a theoretical framework to ensure accuracy. Applying this technique to European country data shows that our method effectively handles data issues without causing loss or distortion, and successfully recovers missing basic reproduction numbers.

Observing the connection between galaxy mass and structure, we have identified an unusual pattern in how colors distribute across massive galaxies. When visualizing the relationship between the NUV-r color and galaxy mass, we find that beyond a critical point around 10^11 solar masses, higher mass galaxies tend to become lighter. This phenomenon represents a shift towards lighter colors, equivalent to a significant and previously unnoted trend not seen in massive elliptical galaxies. To explain this trend, we examined possible causes including star formation, dust, and stellar population variations, utilizing models, existing data, and theoretical frameworks. We found that while star formation and dust play a role, the most significant contributor to the observed trend is the presence of less mature, blueish massive star clusters within these galaxies.

Multitask learning has demonstrated success in learning multiple related tasks simultaneously, and this paper explores its application to a cross-lingual sentiment analysis dataset consisting of English and Spanish text. Initially, a neural network was trained on the dataset, and the network's output was found to be effective for sentiment classification in both languages. Subsequently, a second approach was implemented where a neural network is trained on a single task and the output is used to learn a second, related task. The second approach demonstrated superior performance in learning the cross-lingual sentiment analysis task compared to the first approach. The network's output was also visualized using t-SNE to demonstrate its ability to separate positive and negative samples in both languages, and a clustering algorithm was used to further analyze the output. The results of the experiment support the effectiveness of using output visualization to evaluate the performance of the neural network.

A survey conducted using the TESS rotation-faster-than-12-day program led to the discovery of KIC 9267654, a star that may be a rapidly rotating A-type main sequence star with a rotation period of 1.4 days as indicated by its pulsation periods of 004315 and 003660 days detected in the KIC data. However, the star's rotation profile appears unusual given its low oblaturation consistent with a rotation period of over 10 days as estimated from equivalent spectral lines broadening. An intermediate period of around 2 days is needed to align the star's measured and expected chromial velocities, and an even shorter period of less than one day is needed to align the measured and expected rotation periods derived from surface patterns induced by Coriolis forces. Several potential explanations for the unusual rotation profile of KIC 9267654 include measurement errors, magnetical activity, interaction with a companion star or a nearby star, an anomalous rotation period, or an exceptional rotation state that has perhaps evolved to this rapid speed after leaving the zero-age giant branch.

Recent surges in misinformation dissemination via language-based modalities have compelled urgent action. Although sophisticated deep learning techniques have been successful in detecting such information, they fall short in unseen scenarios and are vulnerable to deceptive content. On the other hand, fetching and utilizing related information from inductive sources like search engines and social media could assist in detecting deceptive news but is time-consuming and ineffective due to the volume of search results. To tackle these challenges, our proposed MetaFEND framework integrates a variety of techniques including diverse optimization algorithms, graph neural networks, and the information from inductive sources for detecting deceptive news. We leverage efficient training strategies to process the information from inductive sources and employ an adaptive optimization algorithm to optimize the pipeline that processes and utilizes this information. We optimize the graph neural network pipeline to learn the most effective sequence of technical operations to deploy when detecting fake news and the most appropriate optimizer to use. Evaluating our MetaFEND framework on public datasets like Weibo, Twitter, and Reddit shows its efficient learning capabilities and superior performance in detecting fake news, surpassing several benchmarks and demonstrating its ability to accurately detect both newly emerged events and surges in deceptive content, like the surrogates for the Ukraine conflict and the Asian flu rumor on social media platforms.

A quaternary Golay complementary array pair is considered infeasible when entries are non-zero and ranked between -1 and 2, and the array dimensions exceed $4\times (N-1)$, where $N$ represents a prime number not equal to 2.

A system leveraging deep learning techniques, specifically a CNN architecture known as the U-Net, has been developed to identify and classify areas in medical images that are relevant to navigation during surgical procedures like laparoscopic bile duct cancer operations. The system, which utilizes patient data from previous operations, is fed into a computer network where the CNN model learns to recognize patterns in images that correspond to key regions of interest. Once trained, the CNN segment's the images, isolating the pertinent areas, which are then presented to a system using a instance segmentation approach called Fast Marches. This allows for real-time, accurate depiction of the key regions, facilitating enhanced navigation during the surgery. Overall, this paper highlights the successful integration of artificial intelligence and medical imaging to improve patient outcomes in complex surgical operations.

This work introduces an innovative unsupervised approach to feature learning that can be expanded to a supervised method with minimal modifications. The core concept involves a sequence modeling perspective where the network is recurrent and processed in an end-to-end manner. The learning process is driven by the goal of reconstruction, and in the supervised variant, the objective is enhanced by incorporating labels during the reconstruction phase. This technique has been successfully tested on various tasks including character and word-level spelling tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness. The method's performance is particularly notable in character-level spelling tasks when using one-hot encoded inputs.

Machine learning models that have been trained on data consisting of knowledge graph triples, such as (entity, relationship, entity), are highly effective in addressing closed-world entity resolution questions. However, these triple-based models struggle with open-world scenarios where the answer may not be documented in the knowledge graph. To bridge this gap, we explored the feasibility of utilizing Large Scale Knowledge Graphs, specifically the WikiKnowledgeGraph, to train and develop new single-turn factual questions and answers from the knowledge graph. We created a dataset comprising 100 million (entity, attribute description, entity) triples and tested various Transformer-based models that include the (Triple-Based, Text-Based, and Pre-trained) architectures. Our standout contribution, Triple-D, stands out as the first (Scale-KG + Transformer) based model to excel in handling open-world FGAs and achieves state-of-the-art results both in English and Chinese, demonstrating that pre-training on massive knowledge graphs is highly effective for tackling single-turn fact-based queries.

This study investigates how a non-linear charge parameter from the context of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) affects the properties of black hole shadows and their connection to thermal radiation. Specifically, it examines extremal Reissner-Nordstrom and extremal Kerr black holes, as well as their charged and spinning counterparts under the influence of a Plankian thermal profile. To analyze the effects of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter, numerical simulations were carried out for various values of this parameter and different ratios of charge to mass. The results show that as the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter increases, the shadow size of black holes decreases. Notably, for a given value of this charge parameter, the shadow size of a charged black hole is found to be smaller than that of a spinning black hole with the same mass. Furthermore, the research reveals that both charge and non-linearity have a significant impact on the thermal profile of black hole horizons, causing a shrinkage in the profile's radius as the Yang-Mills non-linearity and charge-to-mass ratio increase. Given the visual differences observed in shadow images and thermal profiles under varying charge to mass ratios and non-linear charge parameters, it is suggested that observing a black hole's shadow and its thermal profile could provide a method for measuring the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter.

Quantum phenomena such as entanglement enhancements and squeezings are effectively visualized using optical tomograms, with non-Gaussian processing techniques revealing non-classical features. This study investigates entanglement variations and quantum reconstruction techniques for an optical system influenced by laser cooling and non-linear effects, comparing both end-to-end and truncated systems. A specific configuration of the system demonstrates that quantized non-linear properties can be verified through optical tomograms alone, eliminating the need for sophisticated processing methods. This finding suggests that features inherent in non-linear systems, when configured appropriately, inherently possess non-Gaussian characteristics.

This letter reports on the measurement of the branching fractions for the $B^0_s \to K^- K^+$ and $B^0_s \to K^- \pi^+$ decays, performed using data from the LHCb experiment. For both decay modes, the branching fraction determination is influenced significantly by the branching fraction of the $K^*0 \to K\pi$ decay. As a result, direct comparisons with measurements of other $B$ meson decays into related particles, such as the $B^0 \to K^- \pi^+$ decay, are complicated by uncertainties related to hadron models.

To reconstruct the lattice of submodules for a module acting upon it, beginning with a known composition factor lattice that has an associated, known semisimple ring, we focus on a multiplicity-free module. A detailed examination of the submodule lattice's structure, with an example of its application, is provided. An integrated formula for constructing the submodule lattice is presented, based on the composition factor lattice and the group's action, and is illustrated through an example.

We examine the recurrent operator and its application to biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean space. A specific condition is established for biharmonic hypersuraces to be minimal, considering the operator's properties. Furthermore, we explore the condition under which the recurrent operator influences the behavior of biharmonic hypersuraces.

A novel machine model called the p/q-machine is introduced and studied in this paper. This machine model extends the classic finite automaton by incorporating a p/q-counter, which tracks the rational value obtained by dividing the count of 1s in its input word by the count of 0s and raising the state upon reaching integer values. A novel theoretical result is then presented, linking p/q-recognisable subsets of p-adic integers to those recognisable based on their P/q-norms. Furthermore, a p/q-version of the Seifert-Scheiderberg theorem is proved, and a more advanced version of this theorem is also offered as a p/q-machine recognisable pattern.

This study presents a detailed comparison of the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert (CLN) and the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed (BGL) frameworks that define the behavior of $Z_0$ current form factors in its perturbative range. Both models are evaluated against an extensive set of consistency checks, including asymptotic behavior, sum rules derived from vacuum conservation laws in addition to inputs from model-based approaches and data. Notably, the Asymptotic Sum Rule (ASR) derived by P. Ball and the data on $\\pi\\to nu$ decay rates are utilized to establish bounds within which both BGL and CLN formats should ideally conform. Although the BGL framework is found to align well with these constraints, the CLN format exhibits discrepancies in its end-point values, signaling the need for further investigation. Consequently, we propose modified values for these end-points that satisfy all proposed conditions. Notably, baryon decay rate predictions based on CLN's revised end-point values align seamlessly with those derived from BGL format.

A dynamical system is considered computable when its state evolution can be predicted for any initial condition and time period. Conversely, Lyapunov exponent computability implies the ability to determine the stability of the system. This study explores the contrast between the computability of the dynamics and the computability of the Lyapunov exponent for both continuous and discrete systems. It presents findings on the Lyapunov exponent's reliability when the system is in a bounded state space, as well as the conditions under which the sign of the exponent can be determined.

This study introduces angle functions to a broader class of metric spaces, specifically progressive and bigonable spaces, to develop methods for determining if a given space can be conformally mapped into Euclidean space. It defines conformal distance, monotonicity, and a recursive algorithm to calculate this distance, drawing on existing research. Notably, it proves the conformal distance between two distinct definition frameworks is equivalent and offers expanded conditions for determining conformal embeddability.

We develop a new transformation certification framework, called TPC, that extends existing certification methods for neural network safety against minor changes and applies to complex transformations like rotation, scaling, shearing, and snapping of points in point cloud models. The tPC framework achieves enhanced accuracy after a sequence of transformations and provides a unified theoretical basis for certifying transformation safety. Using the framework, we optimize tPC accuracy against various transformations including combined transformations and random transformations, as well as generate deterministic and random transformation chains to enhance accuracy. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that the optimized framework leads to more robust neural network models with improved stability against transformation attacks while maintaining the certified accuracy against transformations.

Test frameworks play a crucial role in software development by helping programmers detect and correct errors without requiring immediate intervention. While test frameworks traditionally serve a purposeful function, evaluating their effectiveness presents challenges. In a recent study conducted over three months, an automated algorithm was deployed to evaluate the effectiveness of testing environments. The evaluation revealed significant improvements in test frameworks, totaling 16 unpublicized corrections out of 63 confirmed valuable modifications to the testing environment. Furthermore, the evaluations facilitated direct benefits, including a newly discovered bug in the Ballerina language server and real-time feedback on valuable modifications to the test framework.

G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles can be obtained by taking crystalline extensions and reducing them modulo a prime number p. Once the coordinates of a (G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycle) are wrapped in the ring of integers of a number field that contains the decomposition field of p, it becomes possible to apply various tests to determine whether the wrapped (G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycle) represents a valid crystalline extension. This paper focuses on the test developed by Kuroda and presents additional tests, and it examines several examples to demonstrate how to raise the embedding dimension in scenarios where a test fails and in cases where additional tests are needed.

Engineering challenges in the context of structural integrity management have led to an interest in using graphene-fiber-reinforced polymers (GFRP) for creating smart, observable composite materials capable of detecting internal damages through changes in electrical properties. However, alterations in electrical conductivity resulting from damages are often minimal, necessitating an innovative approach involving a genetic algorithm (GA) and a Bayesian neural network (BNN) to enhance the accuracy of damage detection using the piezoresistive effect. The GAs role in optimizing the sensing material's architecture within the composite material, allowing the BNN to map electrical property changes to various damage patterns. Testing the synergy between the piezoresistive effect, bi-stable shape memory alloys (SMA), and self-sensing capabilities within GFRP on a structural application, particularly a wing-like composite material with embedded SMAs for potential active damage recovery. The results demonstrated the capability of this integrated system to detect, localize, and in some cases, recover from different types of impact-induced damage, marking a significant advancement in functional composite materials with active recovery properties.

A novel approach to proving integral identities is presented, utilizing geometric vectors in comparison to conventional scalar applications of Green's and divergence theorems. By illustrating the method through multiple examples and providing a list of additional, unproven, yet vectorially formulated, hypotheses, we demonstrate its efficacy. Embracing these assumptions yields a rich collection of validated integral identities.

Right-angled Artin groups acting on trees were analyzed in detail in recent years, with a key property identified in 2013 by Bestvina, Bromberg, and Rubinstein. They showed that a right-angled Artin group $A_{\Gamma}$ acts on a tree with a specific characteristic if a certain subgraph of its graph $\Gamma$ is separating. We extend this finding in two significant ways. First, we prove that if a subgraph of $\Gamma$ is not subcollecting, the group $A_{\Gamma}$ cannot act on a tree in a linear manner. Second, we show that if the group $A_{\Gamma}$ acts on a tree with a specific characteristic, any corresponding convex subgraph of the tree also supports this action. These results are vital for understanding the action of right-angled Artin groups on trees and their relationship with geometric group theory.

This research focuses on accelerating the Nested Neumann algorithm for solving large-scale linear systems Ax=b, particularly when the matrix A is symmetric positive semi-definite and has low rank. We propose using an accelerated version of the Nested Neumann algorithm, incorporating the idea of inception, to reduce the convergence time. Specifically, we examine how different inception depths affect the convergence rate. Additionally, we conduct experiments on several large-scale, real-world datasets to determine the optimal inception depth and make an inception depth selection guideline for the inception-accelerared Nested Neumann algorithm.

We establish new lower bounds on the minimum communication required in contextual linear bandit problems, with or without knowledge of the underlying distribution. Notably, we demonstrate that even with full knowledge of the context distribution, linear elimination methods like Least Squares are not always optimal, and we provide optimized variants with reduced communication needs. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm named $\\tilde{\\text{LS}}$ that achieves optimal regret and meets the lowest possible communication requirements, whether the context distribution is known or unknown. Notably, we prove that $\\tilde{\\text{LS}}$'s total regret is bounded by the information theoretetic limit of the protocol, and we discuss the practical implications of these findings.

To accurately predict particle growth and cooling behavior in protoplanetary disks, a detailed dust model is required. A new radiative-transfer code has been developed to predict the thermal structure of disks by directly solving the radiation-transfer equation for various dust compositions, sizes, and spectra. This code, when paired with physics-based models of gravity, disk shear, and stellar radiation, enables the exploration of evolution and behavior of protoplanetary disks. In a study of a 1 AU scale patch of a disk around AS 2056, it was found that without growth and replenishment of small dust sizes, significant depletion of them occurs due to settling and settling-induced cooling inefficiency. However, if a cycle of growth and replenishment of small dust sizes is in place, larger particles can effectively cool the disk and trigger ice line collapse, which can drive hydrodynamical instabilities that redistribute material and prevent low dust growth efficiencies. The resulting data on millimeter opacity can be integrated over a disk to predict overall emission, explaining observed excess emissions in some disks with low millimeter dust masses. Additionally, the study found that without a cycle of growth and replenishment of small dust sizes, some disks with extremely low millimeter dust masses may become transparent at visible wavelengths, making them prone to rapid ice line collapse and disk dispersal.

A recent result by Li and Souckar establishes a linear growth condition for harmonic functions on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons. Building upon this finding, we establish the asymptotic normality of polynomial growth harmonic functions on such solitons. Specifically, for a soliton $M$ with degree $\mu$ of harmonic function growth, we show that as time progresses, the scaled heat semigroup converges to a heat equation in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The coefficients of this heat equation are determined by the asymptotic behavior of the harmonic function and its normal derivative at infinity. Consequently, harmonic functions with polynomial growth can be fully characterized by initial and boundary conditions, either globally or near infinity.

Neural network classifiers can be manipulated to act in a specific way upon adding a specific pattern to the input, which is known as a backdoor trigger. Recently, triggers that function immediately after a dynamic change in input data have been discovered. Although effective, research so far has focused on specific classification tasks like image and speech recognition. It has proven challenging to create dynamic triggers that work across different classification tasks and even more so when a defense system is in place. We develop a universal dynamic backdoor trigger called DYB that can be implemented in various classification tasks, both simple and complex, including those with advanced security measures. Our DYB trigger works after random changes to the input data, such as noise, cropping, and resizing, and is highly effective against different types of complex attacks. In tested scenarios, the compromised neural network classifier accurately classified inputs with the DYB trigger embedded, even in the presence of defenses like Poisoned Gradient Descent and CleanSGD. Additionally, analysis shows that the DYB trigger remains undetected by both model and data-centric defense mechanisms with a high confidence level. Our findings also demonstrate the effectiveness of the DYB trigger in various scenarios, including multi-step attacks, different optimization algorithms, and training subsets, all while maintaining accurate classification of triggered inputs. The code corresponding to our methodology is publicly available at https://github.com/PuyuWu/UniversalDynamicBackdoor.

This research presents a novel distributed learning algorithm called Random Walk EGG, designed to address inefficiencies in learning models across devices with large datasets. The key idea involves devices communicating less frequently by allowing a random walk approach, where data stays on the device and only gradients are shared occasionally. The random walk strategy is controlled by a parameter called the mixing time, which determines how often devices should communicate. Theoretical analysis shows that the random walk approach incurs slightly higher learning inefficiencies but offers significant benefits by reducing communication costs. The research also provides performance guarantees for the proposed algorithm, with theoretical bounds on its performance. Experimental results further validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, demonstrating its suitability for efficient distributed learning on data that stays on the device.

Recent advances in medical image segmentation rely on utilizing unlabeled data, with new methods emerging to handle class imbalance. Building on these trends, this work proposes a straightforward yet effective regularization technique for semi-supervised learning in medical image segmentation. Quantum correlations within single-particle entangled coherent states have been shown to exhibit nonlocal behavior and enable distance-independent quantum state reconstruction, as demonstrated in recent experiments. Building on these findings, we explore the role of single-particle entanglement in enabling quantum state steering within split optical tables. Our theoretical analysis utilizes an entropy-based measure of correlations and confirms that nonlocal behavior and the ability to remotely determine quantum states are intimately linked. Furthermore, we extend our investigation to multi-particle systems and show that single-particle entanglement can enhance both nonlocal effects and the ability to determine quantum state remotely. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the characteristics of single-particle entanglement.

This paper integrates the Blockchain and Internet of Vehicles (IoVT) technologies to enhance the security and privacy of in-vehicle communication systems. A novel Blockchain-based authentication protocol, called B-PCA, is introduced to safeguard IoVT systems against various attacks and verify the legitimacy of vehicles, NV2Us, and RSUs. B-PCA leverages the inherent properties of Blockchain to self-heal from potential failures caused by attacks and employs cryptographic techniques to protect vehicle data and prevent attacks like replay, spoofing, and man-in-the-middle. A simulation framework is built using the IOTA-Wallet-Python to evaluate the proposed system's efficiency, reliability, and resilience against attacks. The simulation results demonstrate that the B-CA system outperforms existing methods in terms of vehicle, NV2U, and RSU credibility, as well as transaction and block success rates, while also exceeding the security standards set by Information Theory.

This research presents a novel hybrid distributed long short-term memory model, high-throughput hardware design, and a compilation system optimized for hardware. Our proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture leverages a sophisticated decomposition technique called Fourier Heat Kernel to reduce complexity in the model before implementing it on hardware with maximum efficiency. Evaluations conducted on various datasets demonstrate that our FDHT-LSTM model outperforms traditional tensor-decomposed hardware and other advanced neural network models in terms of throughput and energy efficiency, achieving a 3x to 4x improvement over state-of-the-art designs. Additionally, a new FDHT_LSTM framework has been integrated into a hardware-oriented compiler system called TorchT, facilitating seamless deployment of the model on hardware platforms.

We resolve the bateman-horn conjecture for function fields, and obtain precise estimates for the sizes of sets of rational functions with certain properties. Let $K = k(\x)$ be the field of rational functions over the field of constants $k$. We denote the set of irreducible polynomials in $K$ that have degree at most $d$ as $\mathcal{P}_{\le d}$. For a subset $S$ of $\mathcal{P}_{\le d}$, we define $N_s(t)$ to represent the count of rational functions $\fp \in \mathcal{O}_p/\pmat^{n}$ that satisfy specific conditions related to the polynomials in $S$ and a given place $\pmat$ of $K$. If the set $S$ meets certain conditions, we derive asymptotic formulas for $N_s(t)$ as $t$ approaches infinity, similar to those found in previous research over fields of integers. These asymptotic formulas enable us to determine the Galois group of the field extension obtained by adding all rational functions that satisfy the given conditions, with respect to the field $k(\x,...,\x)^{(n-1)}$. We also provide precise estimates for the error terms in the asymptotic formulas.

This research focuses on solving the Schrödinger equation initially at rest and subject to a positive constraint in a bounded region. It proves that a solution will become unbounded (blow up) under certain conditions on the constraint, extending previous findings that applied to infinite spaces. It also establishes additional collapse criteria for solutions within a bounded region.

We develop a unified framework that integrates techniques from both zero and non-zero characteristic, with applications in reduction theories, parameter ideals, and adjacent ideals. We introduce generalized Hartshorne's and Laksov's ideals to define generalized canonical and residual modules, and we define generalized canonical ideals. We also introduce the concepts of persistent and stable ideals, and demonstrate that for any ideal, a subset of it can be identified to form a stable ideal. We establish that certain subsets of ideal powers constitute ideal powers of a single ideal, known as the persistent ideal. We define the persistent multiplicity and persistent type, and in positive characteristic, we prove their limits converge to the analytic spread and type dimension respectively. We further define the persistent Rees ring and show its connection to the usual Rees ring in non-zero characteristic. We also discuss the relationship between these ideals and ideals introduced by Traverso and Seshadri.

A key aspect of Bayesian decision theory is its application in determining the optimal hypothesis through utility functions. In a study performed on hypothesis selection, we examine the approach of using utility functions within a Bayesian framework, particularly in scenarios where the set of possible hypotheses is vast. We compare two utility models: one that assigns distinct utilities to each possible hypothesis, and another that assigns utilities based on groups of related hypotheses. We analyze the decision-making process for both approaches and apply them to a Bayesian linear classification problem, as well as a study on the optimal design of experiments under the same conditions.

Discourse markers play a crucial role in connecting ideas within text, yet analyzing their meanings is challenging due to the varied ways they convey semantic relationships. Existing datasets for studying discourse marker meanings mostly focus on specific types of relationships, leaving a gap in understanding the full range of possibilities. To address this, our team created DiscSense, a comprehensive dataset comprising 1.1 million annotated instances of discourse marker occurrences on Wikipedia, categorized into 51 semantic relations using a combination of machine learning techniques, computational screening, and manual verification. Currently, DiscSense is the most extensive public available dataset for analyzing discourse marker meanings. Evaluations conducted on different models for predicting semantic relationships highlight the value of our proposed framework for classification. Furthermore, we applied the dataset to predict discourse marker meanings and analyze patterns within the data, showcasing the potential usefulness of our proposed framework in real-world scenarios.

We extend the Jordanian twist concept to a more complex scenario with parameters (a,b). Starting with specific initial conditions, we derive modified classical r-matrix properties analogous to those found in the basic case where a/b=1. Specifically, the modified Lennard-Jones (6,8) potential function exhibits invariance under symmetry transformations for the (1,1) case. Additionally, generalized versions of the classical Yang-Lang and Yang-Double-Long twist functions are explored, showing that only the Yang-Double-Long twist remains invariant under reduction to constant and linear approximations.

We develop a fully symbolic decision procedure that determines if one regular expression is contained within another, based on Brzozowski's operator. Our algorithm, evaluated through various test sets, demonstrates superior efficiency compared to existing methods that compare regular expressions for equality or determine their language membership. Our approach outperforms these methods by avoiding the explicit construction of finite automata, and compares favorably with a recent decision tree-based method by Forster et al. That method, while effective for small subsets of operators, incurs exponential costs for certain inputs, a limitation our operator-based algorithm overcomes.

We examine the operator content of Conformal Field Theory in two dimensions (CFT$_{2}$) by mapping it to free fields in three-dimensional Anti-de Sitter space (AdS$_{3}$), focusing on understanding higher-point correlation functions through classical gravity. We develop a unified framework that connects to both the Fock space and Conserved Current Conformal Block expansions. Within this Ads/CFT code, we define geodesic operators in both AdS$_{2}$ and AdS$_{3}$, and analyze their conjugate representations when dealing with conserved currents. We derive a reformulated Fock space representation in which correlation functions map directly to geodesic distances, and extend this understanding to the Ads/CFT context by defining a Conserved Current Geodesic Block expansion for operators defined on geodesics in AdS$_{3}$. We also preview a similar block for Ads$_{2}$.

On 2024-05-20, a cross-shaped detector consisting of ten lobster-eye optics systems was launched on the X-ray Telescope portion of the Chinese Space Station to study transient X-ray events and steady X-ray sources. Within this cross-like configuration, a specific setup with five lobster-eye optics systems is highlighted, where a coordinate system is defined with the vertical and diagonal segments aligned 0 and pi/4 radians respectively. Due to the cross-like image's symmetry, only a segment from -pi/10 to pi/10 radians needs to be analyzed to fully understand the entire system's characteristics. To achieve this, the image is rotated azimuthally in 10-degree increments, and a method is used to identify the specific segment being observed at each increment. The detection efficiency of the system is determined from the reconstructed images, and a uniform X-ray source is simulated to verify its accuracy. Furthermore, the system's capability to localize transient X-ray events is verified, demonstrating a precision of about ten degrees in both longitude and latitude. Given the system's unique structure and its position on the Chinese Space Station, which experiences orbital dynamics including rotation and deformation, precise measurement and reconstruction of images are crucial, making this setup with five lobster-eye optics systems the most compact wide-field X-ray telescope to achieve this precision.

Researchers have developed an universal halo mass function model that connects large-scale structure and dark matter halos, even for a dark matter type with a significant response to scalar perturbations. This research uses a purely density-based neural network to analyze dark matter simulation data from a modified $\Lambda$CDM$ framework, where the impact of scalar perturbations is even more intense. After a initial mass threshold, which may shift under different simulation parameters, the structure formation process collapses, resulting in halos that are lighter and that form earlier. Despite an increased halo mass discrepancy with galaxies, which could lead to bias in studies on the structure of dwarf galaxies and star formation, this issue can be overcome by adjusting the simulation framework to a mass-concentration relation that aligns with observations. This adjustment results in halos that are denser, which could already be present in simulations with only dark matter, potentially eliminating the need for sophisticated orbital modeling to resolve the issues with ultra-faint dwarf galaxies.

This research demonstrates the sensitivity required to detect even the most minimal local magnetic fields in an atomic interferometry system. To achieve this, the system employs quantum state enhancement to reach a sensitivity of $10^{-13}$ Gauss per square root of second, allowing the detection of tidal forces but also highlighting the need for magnetometer isolation or shielding in future astronomical interference experiments.

A theoretical spin-dependent atomic orbital theory is used to analyze the electronic and YSR characteristics of individual magnetic atoms and pairs on copper surfaces with different crystal orientations. We investigate YSR state placements in relation to spin-orbit interaction strength in Cu(001), Cu(010), and Cu(11-3) surfaces, as well as YSR state YSR state shifts caused by changing the distance between magnetic adatoms or dimers. Notable spin-state dependent YSR characteristic differences are observed when comparing Fe and Co adatoms and dimers. Significant YSR state position variations in relation to spin-orbit interaction strength are noted, along with YSR state absence or presence based on the spacing between Fe adatoms or dimers.
